data.plain: Writing a live fact into prose without its `as_of` date, the inputs it came from and a way to recompute it.

analogy.boundary: The picture only shows that painted text falls out of date; it says nothing about whether the live board itself is right.

a note saying when this time was correct

analogy.text: Painting a train's departure time onto a permanent sign instead of showing it on the live board, so the sign keeps the old time after the timetable changes.

reader.counterexample: A page says "the system has 77 components" as a plain fact; the number was right when typed, but nothing records when it was read or how to recompute it, so it still reads as current long after it changed.
reader.does_not_prove: Blocking undated figures leaves open whether the dated ones are still current.

example.text: The fact-claim audit blocks a changing count that was written without a date, source and recompute route, so the figure is not accepted as fact just because it was once true.

reader.governs: Any changing value written into lasting text.
reader.plain: The mistake of writing a changing number or a 'current' status into permanent text as if it were fixed, with no note of when it was read, where it came from or how to work it out again.
reader.potential_misread: That a number true when it was written down stays a reliable fact afterwards.
reader.refuses: Writing a count, a 'current' state or a live total into text with no date, source or way to recompute it.
reader.requires: A date, a named source and a way to recompute the value, or else keeping it out of permanent text or labelling it a dated snapshot.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps readers from trusting an out-of-date figure that looks exactly like a current one.
